title: Adaptive phase-fission scheduler with utility heuristics for latency-sensitive workloads
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Prefill/decode scheduling currently uses static phase-splitting heuristics and kernel affinity hints. We observe tail-latency spikes for mixed workloads where high-throughput batching and low-latency interactive requests contend for the same GPU kernels. Problem: static rules either favor throughput (larger, combined phases that improve kernel utilization) or favor latency (aggressive splitting that increases kernel-launch overhead and hurts throughput). Goal: implement an adaptive phase-fission scheduler that computes a per-phase 'utility score' (U) combining latency sensitivity, kernel cost, KV-cache hit probability, and attention sparsity characteristics to decide when and how to split phases at runtime. The scheduler should: 1) minimize P95/P99 latency regressions for latency-SLO traffic; 2) reclaim throughput when allowed by workload mix; 3) gracefully degrade by falling back to current conservative splitter if inputs are noisy. Key ideas: - Utility function U = w_lat * SLA_penalty + w_cost * kernel_latency_est + w_kv * (1 - kv_hit_rate) + w_sparse * sparsity_reward; weights adapt via online bandit updates. - Use lightweight kernel probes to estimate relative cost of candidate kernels (int8 vs fp16 vs sparse kernels) per phase and bias splitting decisions to align microbatches with kernel-friendly shapes. - Introduce a 'fission budget' per GPU to cap the number of extra kernel launches per second to bound throughput impact. - Run AB experiments with canary pool (dedicated low-traffic GPU pool) and synthetic mixes to estimate net TPS and latency trade-offs. Trade-offs considered: - More aggressive splitting reduces latency for short sequences but increases kernel launch overhead and harms throughput; we mitigate with fission budget and adaptive weights. - Kernel probing adds a small meta-cost and must be rate-limited. - Bandit adaptation introduces non-determinism; need reproducible seeded experiments for offline validation. Implementation scope: - Scheduler core: new scheduler stage that computes U and outputs split plan. - Kernel probe library: small runtime component to query kernel cost for typical seq-len x beam combos. - Metrics: per-request utility, split_count, kernel_launch_rate, simulated throughput loss, per-SLA latency. - Remote config flags and rollout gates.

Why this is different: Prior tickets focused on static phase-windowing, proportional fairness, and deadline-based partitioners. This ticket combines kernel-selection signals, KV-cache heuristics, and online utility optimization to make per-request split decisions, with explicit budgets to preserve throughput in production.
acceptance_criteria: New scheduler stage builds and can be enabled behind runtime flag
Unit and integration tests for utility calculation and budget enforcement
Synthetic benchmark: <5% TPS regression on 80th percentile throughput mix, while reducing P99 latency by >=10% on latency-sensitive mix
Canary rollout in dedicated pool showing stable behavior for 48h before broader rollout
Dashboard panels showing per-phase utility distribution, kernel probe heatmaps, and fission budget metrics
benchmarks: Baseline: mixed 60/40 throughput/interactive trace measured on r5-gpu with runtime-1.19
Synthetic latency trace: median seq=16, 95th seq=64; run against canary pool to measure P95/P99 improvement
Ablation: disable KV component, disable kernel probe, compare utility-weight learning vs fixed weights
rollout_plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag. 2) Run offline replay experiments on replay-cluster for two weeks. 3) Enable in canary dedicated pool (low-traffic GPUs) for 48h with alerting. 4) Gradual ramp to 10% then 50% capacity with rollback thresholds (P99 increase >2x or TPS drop >8%). 5) Full rollout to runtime-1.20 when stable.
